title: Power and sample size
objectives: Compute the power of a test and choose a sample size.

screens.prose: A desk tries a new execution algorithm on 25 orders. If it works, it saves 0.2 basis points per order, with an sd of 1 bp. We test $H_0$: no saving, and reject when $z > 1.645$. If the saving is real, $z$ follows the $H_1$ curve.
screens.question: If the saving is real, about how likely is the test to reject $H_0$?

options.why: 95% is $1 - \alpha$, the chance of keeping $H_0$ when it is true. Under $H_1$, most of the curve sits left of the cut-off.
5% is $\alpha$, the chance of rejecting when there is no saving. The $H_1$ curve has more past the cut-off.
That needs $H_1$ centred on the cut-off. Its centre, 1, is left of 1.645.

hints.text: Rejecting means $z$ lands past 1.645. Under $H_1$, how much of the curve is there?
The shaded part of the $H_1$ curve is the chance of rejecting.
$H_1$ is centred at 1, so the cut-off is 0.645 sd above its centre. About a quarter of a normal lies that far up.

feedback.correct: Only about a quarter of the $H_1$ curve lies past the cut-off.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the shaded part of $H_1$ with the whole curve.

explain.text: Under $H_1$ the statistic is centred at $0.2\sqrt{25} = 1$, left of the cut-off. The test rejects only in the shaded tail: $\Phi(1 - 1.645) = 0.26$. With 25 orders it usually misses a real saving.

screens.prose: Now drag $n$, the number of orders in the test. The cut-off stays at 1.645. Watch where the $H_1$ curve sits, and the shaded share past the cut-off.

derive.caption: $n$ = {{n}} orders: $H_1$ centred at {{fixed(k*sqrt(n), 2)}}, chance of rejecting = {{fixed(values.power, 3)}}

options.why: At 40 orders the caption shows a chance near 0.35. Keep going.
At 100 orders the chance is about 0.64. You need more.
At 400 the chance is 0.99. 80% arrives much sooner.

feedback.correct: Near 155 orders the shaded share reaches 0.80.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag $n$ until the caption reads about 0.800.

explain.text: More orders push the $H_1$ centre, $0.2\sqrt n$, further right while $H_0$ stays put. The centre has to reach about 2.49 for 80%. That happens at $n \approx 155$.

screens.prose: The chance of rejecting $H_0$ when $H_1$ is true is the **power** of the test, $1 - \beta$. Under $H_1$, $z$ is centred at $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma$, here $0.2\sqrt n$. Useful values: $\Phi(0.355) = 0.639$, $\Phi(2) = 0.977$.
screens.question: What is the power with 100 orders?

hints.text: Where is the $H_1$ curve centred when $n = 100$?
The centre is $0.2\sqrt{100} = 2$. Power is the $H_1$ area past 1.645.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the centre of $H_1$, then the area past 1.645.

byKey.beta: 0.361 is $\beta$, the part of $H_1$ left of the cut-off. Power is the part past it.
byKey.no-cutoff: $\Phi(2)$ measures from the centre to 0, not to the cut-off. Subtract 1.645 first.
byKey.alpha: 0.05 is $\alpha$, measured under $H_0$. Power is measured under $H_1$.

explain.text: With 100 orders, $H_1$ is centred at 2, which is 0.355 past the cut-off. So power $= \Phi(0.355) = 0.639$. Four times the data, from 25 to 100, took power from 0.26 to 0.64.

screens.prose: Suppose the algorithm saves nothing, so $\delta = 0$. Watch the $H_1$ curve. Any sample size gives the same picture.
screens.question: What is the power of the test now?

hints.text: Where does the $H_1$ curve sit when $\delta = 0$?
With $\delta = 0$ the $H_1$ curve lies on top of the $H_0$ curve.
The chance of passing 1.645 is now the $H_0$ tail, which is $\alpha$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $\delta = 0$, $H_1$ and $H_0$ are the same curve.

byKey.zero: You expected the test never to reject when there is nothing to find. It still rejects 5% of the time, by luck.
byKey.keep: 0.95 is the chance of keeping $H_0$. Power is the chance of rejecting.
byKey.old: That was the power with a 0.2 bp saving. With no saving the $H_1$ curve has moved.

explain.text: With $\delta = 0$ the $H_1$ curve sits on the $H_0$ curve. The test rejects only by luck, so power $= \alpha = 0.05$. No sample size can raise it.

screens.prose: For 80% power, the $H_1$ centre must sit $z_\beta = 0.842$ past the cut-off $z_\alpha = 1.645$. So we need $0.2\sqrt n = 1.645 + 0.842$.
screens.question: How many orders is that? Round up to a whole order.

hints.text: Solve $0.2\sqrt n = 2.487$ for $\sqrt n$ first.
Square it: $n = 12.435^2 = 154.6$. Round up, since 154 orders fall just short.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 2.487 by 0.2, then square.

byKey.no-square: That is $\sqrt n$. Square it to get $n$.
byKey.no-zbeta: You set the centre on 1.645 plus nothing. That gives 50% power; 80% needs the extra 0.842.
byKey.flipped: You multiplied by 0.2 instead of dividing. A small effect needs many orders, not few.
byKey.rounded-down: 154 orders give power just under 0.80. Round a sample size up.

explain.text: $\sqrt n = 2.487/0.2 = 12.435$, so $n = 154.6$, and we round up to 155. That matches what you found with the slider.

screens.prose: The desk had already run the 25-order test. The result was not significant. The head of trading wrote: “The new algorithm does nothing.”
screens.question: What does the result actually show?

options.text: Little: a real 0.2 bp saving would be missed 74% of the time

options.why: You read a miss as proof of no effect. With power 0.26, missing a real saving is the likely outcome.

options.text: There is a 95% chance the algorithm saves nothing
options.why: You turned $1 - \alpha$ into a chance about the algorithm. 0.95 is the chance of keeping $H_0$ if it is true.

options.text: The saving must be below 0.2 bp
options.why: A real 0.2 bp saving gives this result 74% of the time. The data cannot rule it out.

hints.text: If the saving were real, how often would this test fail to reject?
That chance is $\beta$, the shaded part of $H_1$.
$\beta = 1 - 0.26 = 0.74$. A miss is what we would usually see even if the saving is real.

feedback.correct: Not significant, with power 0.26, says very little.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out how often a real saving would also give a non-significant result.

byKey.nothing: You read a non-significant result as no effect. That reading needs high power, and this test had only 0.26.

explain.text: Under $H_1$ this test keeps $H_0$ with chance $\beta = 0.74$. So “not significant” was the likely outcome even with a real saving. A miss is evidence of no effect only when power is high.

screens.prose: You moved the $H_1$ centre to $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma$ and read off the area past $z_\alpha$: $$1 - \beta = \Phi\left(\frac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma} - z_\alpha\right), \qquad n = \left(\frac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)\,\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2.$$ At 5% and 80% power, $z_\alpha = 1.645$ and $z_\beta = 0.842$.
screens.question: What is $(1.645 + 0.842)^2$, the constant in front of $(\sigma/\delta)^2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two $z$ values, then square the sum.

byKey.no-square: That is the sum. Square it.
byKey.sum-squares: You squared each term and added. Square the sum instead.

explain.text: $(1.645 + 0.842)^2 = 2.487^2 = 6.185$, or 6.18 with unrounded $z$ values. So $n = 6.18\,(\sigma/\delta)^2$ for 80% power at 5%. Halve the effect and the sample size quadruples.

screens.prose: We derive the power formula. The test rejects when $z = \bar x/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ exceeds $z_\alpha$. Under $H_1$ the true mean is $\delta$, and $Z$ is standard normal.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Power $= P(z > z_\alpha \mid H_1)$: we reject when $z$ passes the cut-off
Under $H_1$, $z = \dfrac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma} + Z$: the mean $\delta$ is divided by the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$
Power $= P\left(Z > z_\alpha - \dfrac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma}\right)$: subtract the shift from both sides

hints.text: Start from what power means.
Next, say what $z$ looks like when $H_1$ is true.
Definition, then the shifted statistic, then subtract the shift, then use symmetry of the normal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line rewrites the one before it.

byKey.s1: The definition of power comes first.
byKey.s2: You need the shifted form of $z$ before you can subtract the shift.
byKey.s3: Subtracting the shift needs the shifted form of $z$ first.
byKey.s4: Symmetry turns an upper tail into $\Phi$, so it comes last.

explain.text: Under $H_1$ the statistic is a standard normal shifted right by $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma$. Power is the chance the shifted normal passes $z_\alpha$. Setting it to $\Phi(z_\beta)$ and solving gives the sample size formula.

screens.prose: `math.erf` gives the normal cdf, as `Phi` in the starter shows. Finish `power` so it returns $\Phi(\delta\sqrt n/\sigma - z_\alpha)$. The loop prints the power at four sample sizes.
screens.question: Complete `power(delta, sigma, n, z_alpha)`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests, each compared with math.isclose. NumPy and SciPy are available but load slowly; this task needs only math.

hints.text: The shift is the $H_1$ centre on the $z$ scale.
`shift = delta * sqrt(n) / sigma`.
Return `Phi(shift - z_alpha)`.

feedback.correct: Your function matches the formula on every test.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Compute the shift $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma$, subtract $z_\alpha$, then apply `Phi`.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that both `...` are replaced.

explain.text:
The loop prints 0.259, 0.639, 0.801 and 0.991. Power climbs fast at first, then flattens as it nears 1. With `delta = 0` the function returns $\Phi(-1.645) = 0.05$, which is $\alpha$.

```python
shift = delta * sqrt(n) / sigma
return Phi(shift - z_alpha)
```

screens.prose: A strategy's true mean daily return is 0.05%, with a daily sd of 1%. We test $H_0$: mean 0, one-sided at 5%, and want 80% power. Use $n = 6.18\,(\sigma/\delta)^2$.
screens.question: How many trading days of returns does the test need?

hints.text: Work out $\sigma/\delta$ first, in the same units.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square $\sigma/\delta$ and multiply by 6.18.

byKey.no-square: You multiplied by $\sigma/\delta = 20$. The formula squares it.
byKey.root: That is $\sqrt n$. Square it to get the number of days.
byKey.flipped: You used $\delta/\sigma$. A small edge needs many days, so the ratio is $\sigma/\delta = 20$.

explain.text: $n = 6.18 \times (1/0.05)^2 = 6.18 \times 400 \approx 2{,}473$ days, about 9.8 years of 252 trading days. The canvas shows 400 days: $H_1$ is centred at only 1. Most backtests are shorter than ten years, so most cannot reliably find an edge this size.

ideas: Power is the chance a test rejects $H_0$ when the effect is real: $1 - \beta$.
Power grows with $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma$: a bigger effect, more data or less noise. With no effect it equals $\alpha$.
For 80% power at 5%, $n = 6.18\,(\sigma/\delta)^2$: halving the effect quadruples the data.

formula.name: Power of a one-sided z test

summary.trap: Not significant is not the same as no effect. With low power, missing a real effect is the likely outcome.

quiz.question: What is the power with 200 orders?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the cut-off from the new centre, then use $\Phi$.

byKey.doubled: You doubled the power with the data. Power is a chance, at most 1, and it grows with $\sqrt n$ through $\Phi$.

explain.text: Doubling $n$ moves the centre by a factor of $\sqrt 2$, from 2 to 2.828. Power rises from 0.639 to $\Phi(1.183) = 0.882$, not to double.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $\delta = 0.01$, square $\sigma/\delta = 49$ and multiply by 6.18.

explain.text: $\sigma^2 = 0.24$ and $\delta^2 = 0.0001$, so $n = 6.18 \times 2{,}400 \approx 14{,}832$ orders. A one-point gain in a rate is a tiny effect, so it needs thousands of trades.

quiz.prose: A test needs 400 days to detect a mean return of 0.1% a day with 80% power.
quiz.question: How many days does it need to detect 0.05% a day with the same power and sd?

feedback.correct: Half the effect needs four times the data: 1,600 days.

byKey.doubled: You doubled $n$ for half the effect. $n$ depends on $1/\delta^2$, so it quadruples.
byKey.halved: A smaller effect is harder to see, so it needs more data, not less.

quiz.prose: The execution test has 100 orders and power 0.639 at $\alpha = 0.05$. The desk relaxes the test to $\alpha = 0.10$, so $z_\alpha$ falls to 1.282.
quiz.question: What happens to the power?

options.text: It falls, because the test is weaker
options.why: A lower cut-off rejects more often, under $H_1$ as well as under $H_0$.

options.text: It stays at 0.639: power depends only on $n$
options.why: Power depends on the cut-off too. Moving it left adds $H_1$ area past it.
$1 - \alpha$ is the chance of keeping a true $H_0$. Power is measured under $H_1$.

feedback.correct: A lower cut-off buys power with more false alarms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the cut-off to 1.282 and find the $H_1$ area past it.

explain.text: Power $= \Phi(2 - 1.282) = \Phi(0.718) = 0.764$. The price is $\alpha$ doubling to 0.10. Power and $\alpha$ rise and fall together for a fixed $n$.
